title: How Node.js really runs JavaScript under the hood
excerpt: Node.js uses V8, libuv and OS kernel primitives to keep a single-threaded JavaScript view while work happens on multiple native threads.
body:
A simple Node.js HTTP server started on a Linux box instantly disproves the textbook claim that “Node runs on a single thread.” Running `ps -eLf` or opening the process in htop shows eight or more native threads belonging to the same PID. Those extra threads are not stray bugs; they belong to the runtime itself. The article Node.js Isn’t Single-Threaded.

How libuv and the OS Kernel Actually Run Your Code walks through the three architectural layers that generate those threads, explains why network sockets never touch the libuv worker pool, and shows how file-system and crypto operations do. By the end of this post the reader will know where the threads live, how the event loop coordinates them, and what that means for writing truly non-blocking code.

## The three tiers of Node.js

Node.js can be split into three distinct layers, each with its own responsibilities and thread model.  
The top tier is the V8 engine, which runs JavaScript on a single “main thread.” All function calls, object allocations, and synchronous loops execute here, so a tight `while (true) {}` or deep recursion will monopolize the CPU and stall everything else.  

Below V8 sits the libuv runtime. It provides two key pieces: a single-threaded event loop that watches timers and I/O callbacks, and a worker thread pool that defaults to four pre-spawned OS threads. When JavaScript invokes an asynchronous API such as `fs.readFile` or `crypto.pbkdf2`, V8 hands the request to libuv, which decides whether the work can stay in the event loop or must be off-loaded to a worker thread.  

The bottom tier is the operating-system kernel. On Linux the epoll subsystem, on BSD/macOS kqueue, and on Windows IOCP monitor thousands of sockets without allocating a thread per socket. These mechanisms wake the Node.js event loop only when a socket becomes readable or writable, keeping the main thread free for JavaScript work.

The source visualises this stack as a vertical flow from JavaScript code down through V8, libuv, and finally the kernel. Each tier adds its own threads, which is why a “single-threaded” Node process actually hosts multiple native threads.

## Network I/O stays out of the libuv worker pool

A common misconception is that every asynchronous call in Node ends up in the libuv thread pool. The source makes it clear that network operations are an exception. When an HTTP server, a PostgreSQL client, or a WebSocket connection is created, the kernel’s event demultiplexer takes ownership of the socket file descriptors. The kernel watches the descriptors for readiness events and notifies the Node event loop via a lightweight wake-up signal.

Because the kernel can handle tens of thousands of sockets without spawning a thread for each, Node can serve massive numbers of concurrent connections while the event loop remains a single thread. This design eliminates the latency spikes that would appear if each network request required a background thread, and it explains why a busy server does not freeze when many clients connect simultaneously.

## File-system and crypto operations use the worker pool

File-system calls and many crypto primitives lack truly non-blocking system interfaces on most operating systems. libuv therefore falls back to its worker threads for those operations. The flow looks like this:

1. JavaScript calls an async API, e.g. `fs.readFile` or `crypto.pbkdf2`.  
2. V8 forwards the request to libuv.  
3. libuv enqueues the request onto the worker thread pool.  
4. A worker thread runs the blocking system call (read, write, hash, etc.).  
5. When the call finishes, the worker posts the result back to the event loop.  
6. The event loop invokes the original JavaScript callback.

```js
import fs from 'node:fs';
fs.readFile('/var/log/app.log', (err, data) => {
  console.log('File read complete:', data.length);
});
```

In this snippet the disk read happens on a background thread, so the main thread stays free to process other callbacks, such as incoming HTTP requests. The source notes that without the worker pool, reading a 4-gigabyte file would block every request, turning the server into a bottleneck.

A similar pattern appears with `crypto.pbkdf2`, which the article cites as a classic “blocking” example. When a password hash is computed, libuv schedules the work on a worker thread, preventing the entire backend from freezing while the hash finishes.

## The six-phase event loop

The article breaks the event loop into six distinct phases that run on the main thread each tick. First, timers scheduled by `setTimeout` or `setInterval` fire. Next, pending callbacks that were deferred to the following iteration run. The third and fourth phases, idle/prepare and poll, are used internally; the poll phase retrieves new I/O events and may block waiting for kernel signals.

After poll, the check phase runs `setImmediate` callbacks, and finally the close callbacks clean up closed handles. Understanding these phases helps developers predict when a callback will fire and why certain operations appear to “lag” under heavy load. For example, a long-running timer can delay the poll phase, causing network readiness events to wait longer before being processed.

## The takeaway

Node.js hides a multi-threaded C/C++ runtime behind a single-threaded JavaScript surface. Network sockets stay in the kernel’s non-blocking subsystem, while file-system and crypto calls run in libuv’s worker pool. Knowing which layer handles a given operation lets developers tune the thread-pool size, avoid accidental thread starvation, and write code that truly scales without surprising pauses.
